# Draft:Biomass-driven agriculture__disambig_1

Biomass-driven agriculture is a term used to describe agricultural systems that emphasize high levels of plant biomass production and retention as a means of supporting soil health, nutrient cycling, and crop productivity. The concept reflects practices documented in cover crop–based systems, high-residue farming, and reduced-tillage approaches, where plant-derived organic matter plays a central role in maintaining soil function. Such systems are commonly associated with Regenerative agriculture, Agroecology, and Conservation agriculture, which similarly prioritize continuous soil cover, minimal disturbance, and biologically driven processes.
Overview
Agricultural systems described as biomass-driven typically focus on increasing both the quantity and continuity of plant-derived material within the soil environment. This includes aboveground biomass, such as crop residues and cover crops, as well as belowground inputs from roots and root exudates. These organic inputs contribute to soil organic matter, which plays a key role in soil structure, water retention, and biological activity.
In these systems, biomass is not treated as a byproduct of production but as a central component of system function. Management practices are often designed to maintain continuous soil cover and reduce the loss or disturbance of organic material.
Scientific basis
The role of biomass in agricultural systems is supported by research on soil organic matter dynamics and plant–soil interactions. Plant-derived organic matter contributes to the formation and stabilization of soil carbon, which is associated with improved soil aggregation, nutrient availability, and resistance to erosion.
The decomposition of plant residues provides a primary energy source for soil microorganisms, which regulate key processes such as nutrient cycling and organic matter turnover. Maintaining residues on the soil surface has been shown to improve environmental quality by reducing runoff, moderating soil temperature, and enhancing water infiltration. Soil biodiversity is also closely linked to the availability of organic inputs, with diverse microbial communities contributing to ecosystem stability and function.
Practices
Practices associated with biomass-focused agricultural systems are widely documented and include cover cropping, residue retention, and reduced soil disturbance.
Cover cropping is used to increase biomass production during periods when cash crops are not actively growing. These crops can contribute to soil fertility, suppress weeds, and improve system resilience. The use of diverse cover crop mixtures has been associated with increased ecosystem multifunctionality.
Residue retention, in which crop residues are left on the soil surface, contributes to soil organic matter accumulation and erosion control. This practice is a defining feature of high-residue agricultural systems.
Reduced-disturbance tillage systems are frequently used alongside biomass-focused practices. No-till farming avoids soil disturbance entirely, allowing residues and biomass to remain on the surface. Reduced-till approaches minimize soil disruption while maintaining some flexibility in field operations. Strip-till systems create narrow tilled zones for planting while leaving most of the soil undisturbed and covered with residue. These approaches help preserve soil structure and support long-term carbon retention.
Mechanical methods for managing high levels of biomass are also used in some systems. Roller-crimpers, for example, are used to terminate cover crops by flattening them into a mulch layer, which can suppress weeds and protect the soil surface.
Relationship to other approaches
Biomass-driven agriculture is not considered a formally defined agricultural system but rather a descriptive framework that overlaps with several established approaches. In conservation agriculture, principles such as minimal soil disturbance, permanent soil cover, and crop diversification align closely with biomass-focused practices. Similarly, regenerative agriculture emphasizes soil health and carbon sequestration through increased biological activity and organic matter inputs.
Agroecology also highlights ecological processes and biodiversity, including the role of plant biomass in sustaining soil systems.
Benefits and limitations
Practices that increase biomass production and retention have been associated with improvements in soil organic matter, water-holding capacity, and biological activity. These changes may contribute to increased resilience to environmental stress and reduced reliance on external inputs.
However, implementation can present challenges, including the need for careful management of crop rotations, planting schedules, and biomass termination. In some cases, specialized equipment may be required, and climatic conditions may limit biomass production.
